info.title: ATLAS API
info.description:
The ATLAS public API (/v1). This document is the single source of truth for the **public** API surface: the client libraries and the reference documentation are generated from it, and a change to an endpoint changes this document in the same release.

**What this contract does not cover.** This document describes the public `/v1` surface. A small number of routes exist outside it for platform operation; they are not part of this contract, are not callable with an API key, and are deliberately undocumented here. Their set is fixed and checked on every build, so it cannot grow by accident.

**Response headers every call carries.** Two sets, described here once because they are properties of the whole surface rather than of any one operation, and OpenAPI has no way to say that.

`X-Request-Id` is on **every** response, success or failure. It is a fresh value per request, minted by ATLAS and never read from the request, and the same value appears in the server-side record of that call — so quoting it in a support report identifies the exact call, whatever its status. This is what to quote for a `403`, a `409` or a `429`. It is distinct from the `errorId` a `500` carries in its body, which references one server-side failure and is the only detail that response discloses.

`RateLimit-Limit`, `RateLimit-Remaining` and `RateLimit-Reset` are on every **authenticated** response outside `/auth/*`, and describe one budget: the **caller's own overall request rate** — the ceiling per window, how many calls are left (floored at zero), and how many seconds until the window restarts. Reading them does not itself consume budget. They describe a **request-rate** limit and never a credit allowance, which is a separate mechanism.

**They describe only that budget, which matters most on a `429`.** Several operations have their own narrower limits — posting to a discussion, writing to the achievements board, rendering an invoice, and the AI features. When one of those refuses, the response still carries the caller's overall figures **unchanged**, so `RateLimit-Remaining` can read a healthy number beside a `429`. Diagnose a refusal from `Retry-After` and the problem's `errorCode`, never from `RateLimit-Remaining`. When the overall budget itself is what refused, `RateLimit-Remaining` reads zero.

**Their absence is not "unlimited".** If the counter backing the budget cannot be reached, ATLAS serves the request rather than failing it, and omits these three headers rather than reporting a figure it cannot stand behind. Treat their absence as unknown. Responses under `/auth/*` never carry them at all: those endpoints refuse with one deliberately indistinguishable shape, and a remaining count would defeat it.

A `429` raised by a request-rate limit carries `Retry-After`, in seconds. Two kinds of `429` do not, because neither clears after an interval: an exhausted AI credit allowance (`ATLAS-BIL-001`/`ATLAS-BIL-002`), which resets daily, and the discussion live-link connection cap (`ATLAS-FRM-010`), which clears when a connection is closed. The `errorCode` distinguishes them, which is why it and not `RateLimit-Remaining` is what to branch on. Every operation a request-rate limit can refuse declares that `429`; the authenticated ones share one description, `Throttled`.

**Paging.** One convention, named here once so a client library generates a single paginator: a bounded `limit` and an opaque `cursor` on the request, and a `{ items: [...], nextCursor: string | null }` envelope on the response, where a null `nextCursor` means the end. The cursor encodes server-side position and a client that parses one is relying on something that will change. Cursor rather than offset because these collections grow while they are being read, and offset paging over a growing table skips and duplicates rows in a way the caller cannot see.

**Three** groups of reads do not follow it yet, and none is a precedent. **Four** operations page with `page` + `size`; that shape is **frozen** — no new operation may use it. **Seven** cap with a bare `limit` and offer no second page, so a caller who reaches the cap cannot get the rest. **Thirteen** return an unbounded top-level array. The last two groups — all twenty array-returning reads — carry `x-atlas-pagination: deferred-j3`; giving them the envelope changes a response shape and is tracked separately. Any new collection endpoint uses the convention above.

**Versioning.** `info.version` above is the version of THIS CONTRACT and is not the ATLAS product version. It moves when the described surface moves — minor for additive change, patch for a correction — and it does not move at a release cut. A breaking change means `/v2`, never an edit to `/v1`. What changed between two versions is recorded in the contract's changelog, published beside this document.

**A body that cannot be read.** Every operation that takes a JSON body answers `400` with `ATLAS-VAL-002` when the body never becomes an object: it is missing, it is not JSON, or a value cannot take its field's type - a string where a number belongs, a name an enum does not know. `ATLAS-VAL-001` is the other half: the body was read, and a field broke one of its stated constraints. Whenever a field can be named, both carry an `errors` array whose `field` says where the problem is - properties dotted, map keys and indices in brackets; a body that is missing, or malformed before any field, has no `errors` array. Neither ever repeats the value that was sent, which on some operations is a password. The operations below declare their own `400`s; this one applies to all of them and is stated once, here.

**The rest of a request that cannot be read.** A path, query or header value that cannot take its type - an id that is not a UUID, a number that is not a number - or a required one that is absent is `400` with `ATLAS-VAL-003`, naming the parameter and never its value (the problem's `instance` is the request's own path, so a path value you sent appears there and nowhere else); a query parameter over its stated bound is `400` with `ATLAS-VAL-001`, like a body field. An address nothing answers at is `404` with `ATLAS-SYS-005`, a method the address does not answer is `405` with `ATLAS-SYS-009`, and a `Content-Type` an operation does not read or an `Accept` it cannot write is `415` or `406` with `ATLAS-SYS-010`. **Every response this API sends as a refusal carries an `errorCode`**, so a client never has to branch on a status alone. The one exception is a path the web server cannot parse at all - an encoded slash (`%2F`) or a NUL byte in it - which is refused `400` with an HTML body before this API sees the request. No address in this contract contains either, so a client that builds its paths from it and encodes each value does not send one.

tags.name: developer
tags.description: Developer accounts - applications, API keys, the learners you link as end users, personalisation for them, sign-in on behalf, webhooks and usage.

tags.name: content
tags.description: The official copy - lectures and their versions and files, the document a lecture becomes, courses, trash, and reporting a problem with a lecture.

x-atlas-derived.rule: Every operation whose security admits a scheme publishing x-atlas-scopes (a developer credential), plus the operation such a scheme names in x-atlas-issued-by. Security requirements naming only a signed-in session are dropped, and so are the schemes they name.
x-atlas-derived.retry: repeatable: an idempotent method (RFC 9110). repeatable-with-key: the operation declares an Idempotency-Key header, and every attempt carries the same key. once: anything else, never retried after a failure that may have reached the server. Every class retries a 429 after its Retry-After, because a throttled request did nothing.

get.summary: Describe the API key making this request
get.description:
Returns the identity of the API key presented on this request - which key, which app, which developer account, and when it stops working. It discloses nothing the caller did not already hold: a leaked key must not become a reconnaissance tool for the account it was taken from.

**It needs no scope**, and it is the only operation that does not: a key has to be able to ask what it is before it can be told what it lacks, and this answer contains nothing the holder was not already holding - including `scopes`, which is its own grant.

Every other key-reachable operation names the scope it costs; a key presented on an operation it does not hold the scope for is refused `403` `ATLAS-SYS-007`, naming the scope required. A key presented on an operation that accepts no key at all is refused `403` `ATLAS-SYS-003`, identically for its own organisation and any other.

Rate-limit state is on the response headers (`RateLimit-Limit`, `RateLimit-Remaining`, `RateLimit-Reset`), where every other endpoint publishes it, rather than in this body.

401.description: No credential was presented, or the key does not authenticate anything - unknown, revoked, expired, or superseded by a rotation whose overlap has closed. One shape for all of them, with no diagnostic detail (`ATLAS-SYS-002`)

403.description: A valid credential that cannot be used here - an access token rather than an API key (`ATLAS-SYS-003`)

post.summary: Swap the code for a pass, or renew one
post.description:
Exchanges a one-time code for a short-lived pass, or renews a pass with a refresh token.

**No credential, and no client secret.** This is called by your server, which holds no ATLAS session; what authorises it is the code or the refresh token in the body. There is no client secret because this flow is for applications acting on a person's behalf, including native and browser clients where a shipped secret is not a secret - PKCE is what binds the exchange instead.

**JSON, not `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`.** This departs from RFC 6749 deliberately: this API's convention is plain JSON and every other operation in this document is JSON, so a single form-encoded endpoint would be the only one in the product and would need its own handling in each generated SDK. The practical consequence is that an off-the-shelf OAuth2 client library will not work against this leg unmodified.

**The refresh token is rotated on every use.** Presenting one that has already been spent is treated as theft: every unspent refresh token under that grant is revoked, so neither holder can renew and the application must send the person through the consent screen again. Already-issued passes keep working until they expire.

Every refusal is one `400` with `ATLAS-DEV-014` - an expired code, a replayed one, a code minted for another application, a `redirect_uri` that does not match the one the code was sent to, a failed PKCE verification and a spent refresh token are indistinguishable. This is the one operation whose failures a caller can drive in a loop, so it does not report which half of a credential pair was wrong.

200.description: A delegated pass and its renewal token

400.description: The code or refresh token cannot be exchanged (`ATLAS-DEV-014`)

get.summary: The learners this application has linked
get.description:
Every end user linked by the application whose key you presented. There is no application parameter, and that is deliberate: the credential names the application, so a key cannot reach another one's learners even by asking.

**API key only.** A signed-in person is refused - end users are an integration capability, and admitting a browser session would mean inventing an application-selection parameter that carries none of the ownership the credential gives for free.

403.description: Not a member / no such org (`ATLAS-ORG-002`, no existence oracle), a key without the scope this operation names (`ATLAS-SYS-007`), or a key whose account is not entitled (`ATLAS-SYS-008`)

post.summary: Link one of your own learners
post.description:
Links a learner of yours to the application whose key you presented. ATLAS stores a digest of `ref` and nothing else.

**Linking a learner who is already linked returns the existing link** rather than refusing: that is the state you asked for. Send an `Idempotency-Key` header to make a retry provably act once - the same key with the same body replays the first outcome, and the same key with a DIFFERENT body is refused `409` rather than answered with somebody else's result.

parameters.name: Idempotency-Key
parameters.description: A repeat guard. Optional; when present, 8-255 characters, and unique per distinct request you make.

201.description: The link, new or already existing

400.description: An unusable reference (`ATLAS-DEV-011`) or a malformed `Idempotency-Key` (`ATLAS-DEV-009`)

403.description: Not a member / no such org (`ATLAS-ORG-002`, no existence oracle), a key without the scope this operation names (`ATLAS-SYS-007`), or a key whose account is not entitled (`ATLAS-SYS-008`)

409.description: This `Idempotency-Key` was already used for a different request, or its first call is still in flight (`ATLAS-DEV-010`); or this application has reached the maximum number of live links (`ATLAS-DEV-012`) - revoke one you no longer need

delete.description:
Stops this end user reaching anything. Idempotent: revoking an already-revoked link is the state you asked for, and the transition is one-way at the database - there is no request that restores one.

The row is kept rather than deleted, because billing counts ACTIVE end users per period and a closed period has to stay answerable.

403.description: Not a member / no such org (`ATLAS-ORG-002`, no existence oracle), a key without the scope this operation names (`ATLAS-SYS-007`), or a key whose account is not entitled (`ATLAS-SYS-008`)

404.description: No such link, another application's, or already unreachable (`ATLAS-SYS-005`) - the three are deliberately indistinguishable

post.summary: Personalisation for a linked end user
post.description:
How ATLAS would present content to this learner, given the profile you supply: the features it recommends, the endorsements behind them and the presentation plan.

**POST, and it writes nothing.** The profile is too large and too structured to be a query string, and it is your learner's scores - a value that must not end up in an access log, a browser history or a referrer header, which is what a GET would do to it.

**This is the instant-changes half.** It spends no AI allowance and returns no generated text; the AI-rewrite half is tracked and arrives later. Revoking the link refuses this immediately.

**The profile is held to the instrument before anything reads it.** Build it the way `GET /questionnaire/profile` returns one: the `taxonomyVersion` ATLAS serves, dimension and sub-dimension codes the instrument declares, each sub-dimension in the shape the instrument gives it (`bipolar` or `multi-category`), only categories that sub-dimension has, every score a 1-5 mean, and a score only for a dimension listed in `completedDimensions`. A profile that disagrees is refused with `400` `ATLAS-DEV-020`, whose `errors` names each field that disagrees and never repeats what it said there - the values are your learner's.

200.description: The personalisation ATLAS resolves for that profile

400.description: The profile could not be used, for one of three reasons a caller can tell apart by `errorCode`. `ATLAS-VAL-002`: the body could not be read - not JSON, or a value that cannot take its field's type, such as an unknown `structureType`. `ATLAS-VAL-001`: a field is missing or over its bound. `ATLAS-DEV-020`: the profile is well-formed and disagrees with the instrument - see the operation's description. Each carries an `errors` array naming the fields whenever a field can be named (a body that is not JSON at all has none), and none repeats a value.

403.description: Not a member / no such org (`ATLAS-ORG-002`, no existence oracle), a key without the scope this operation names (`ATLAS-SYS-007`), or a key whose account is not entitled (`ATLAS-SYS-008`)

404.description: No such link, another application's, or revoked (`ATLAS-SYS-005`)

get.summary: API usage for a developer account
get.description:
Calls, the per-app breakdown and where the account stands against its request budget, for the current month to date.

Readable by ADMIN, MODERATOR and USER - a developer User has read-only access to the usage views, and operational allowance state is kept outside commercial data deliberately: it is what explains the product's behaviour to the person experiencing it. Also readable by a key holding `usage:read`.

**No figure here is denominated in money.** Those live on `/dev/usage/credits`, which is Admin-only and which no key reaches.

`rateLimit` is ABSENT when the counter could not be read. Absent means unknown, never "within limits" - do not render an outage as headroom.

403.description: Not a member / no such org (`ATLAS-ORG-002`, no existence oracle), a key without the scope this operation names (`ATLAS-SYS-007`), or a key whose account is not entitled (`ATLAS-SYS-008`)

get.description:
One page of the org's resources, newest first. Open to any member - browsing is what a library is for, and the org scope is what bounds it. In-flight resources ARE listed, with their processing state, rather than hidden. Soft-deleted resources are NOT - they are listed by `/resources/trash`, behind its own Admin/Moderator gate. Filtering by course arrives with that step.

**What a USER sees is narrower than what an Admin/Moderator sees**: a FAILED display version is omitted entirely for a USER - no row and no placeholder - because a learner can do nothing about a failed upload, while retry, re-upload and reading the failure reason are all Admin/Moderator acts. Requesting `status=FAILED` as a USER therefore yields an empty page rather than an error.

This hides fewer resources than it first appears: the display version is current-else-latest and supersede only fires on a READY seal, so a failed v2 over a live v1 still displays the v1 and stays visible to everyone. What a USER loses is a first upload that never succeeded.

parameters.name: status
parameters.description: Restrict to these states; repeat the parameter to pass several. Omitted means all of them. For a USER the result is always intersected with the non-FAILED states (see above).

parameters.name: q
parameters.description:
Keyword search: restrict to resources whose TITLE contains this, case-insensitively. Blank or omitted means all of them.

It NARROWS rather than replaces - it composes with `status`, with the USER rule above, with the org scope and with the trash exclusion, so no search reaches anything the plain listing would not have shown.

`%` and `_` match THEMSELVES; they are not wildcards to the caller.

Searching inside a document's content is a different question answered by meaning rather than substring. It is served for ONE lecture at a time by `POST /o/{orgId}/resources/{resourceId}/search`. An org-wide search inside content still does not exist: it has no single version to authorise against and no per-document bound on its cost, and is tracked separately.

The length ceiling is measured on what you SEND, before the api trims surrounding whitespace - so a 100-character term padded with a space is 101 characters and is refused.

parameters.name: size
parameters.description: Page size; capped so a caller cannot request an unbounded page

400.description: An out-of-range page or size, or a search term over 100 characters

403.description: Not a member / no such org (`ATLAS-ORG-002`, no existence oracle)

get.summary: Get a short-lived URL for the original file
get.description:
Mints a presigned GET URL for the resource's original bytes (the "download original" action). Any member may download what their org holds. The bytes come straight from object storage, never through the api.

The URL forces `Content-Disposition: attachment` and `application/octet-stream`, so an uploaded HTML or SVG file downloads rather than rendering - uploaded bytes are untrusted. Minted per request and short-lived; re-request rather than caching it.

200.description: The download URL and when it lapses

403.description: Not a member / no such org (`ATLAS-ORG-002`)

404.description: No such resource in this org (`ATLAS-SYS-005`, no existence oracle)

409.description: The resource is not READY, so there are no sealed bytes to download (`ATLAS-CNT-008`) - it is still processing, or its upload failed and the bytes were discarded.

451.description: The file has been taken down (`ATLAS-CNT-016`): a super admin upheld a copyright or abuse report against these exact bytes, so the fingerprint is blocklisted and every org holding the file loses access together - not only the org that was reported. Deliberately NOT disguised as a 404: a takedown notice is given openly, never silently, and the caller is being told about their own content. The remedy is an appeal, not a retry.

get.description: The resource's status and, once the upload is confirmed, its size. Any member may read; a cross-org id reads as 404 (no existence oracle). The bytes' fingerprint is computed and stored server-side but is deliberately not returned — see `ResourceResponse`.

403.description: Not a member / no such org (`ATLAS-ORG-002`, no existence oracle)

404.description: No such resource in this org (`ATLAS-SYS-005`, no existence oracle)

post.description:
Sent when a resource's first version finished processing and became the official copy.

Fetch the resource with `getResource` to read its title, versions and block tree; this message carries ids and nothing else, because a webhook body leaves ATLAS for a machine on the public internet and nothing derived from an uploaded document travels without a reason.

You will receive this for EVERY route to READY, including when the same bytes were already processed for somebody else and ATLAS reused the result. There is no way to tell the two apart, and that is deliberate.

2XX.description: Any 2xx means you accepted it and ATLAS stops trying. Answer as soon as you have durably recorded the message, and do the work afterwards - ATLAS gives you ten seconds.

default.description: Anything that is not a 2xx - including a redirect, which ATLAS does not follow - is a failure and will be retried.

post.summary: A lecture was replaced by a newer version
post.description:
Sent when a new version superseded one that was already the official copy. `data.version_id` is the new one.

Distinct from `resource.ready` because the difference cannot be recovered afterwards: once the pointer has moved, nothing in the data says whether this was a first publication or a replacement, and version numbers cannot answer it either.

2XX.description: Any 2xx means you accepted it and ATLAS stops trying

default.description: Anything else is a failure and will be retried

post.summary: A lecture could not be processed
post.description:
Sent when processing failed terminally. That version will never become the official copy, and nothing further will be attempted for it.

**Subscribe to this one.** Without it, a pipeline waiting for `resource.ready` waits for ever on a document that cannot be parsed, and polling is the only way to find out - which is the thing this section exists to replace.

`data.reason` is ATLAS's own name for the stage that refused. It is never a parser message and never a byte of the document.

2XX.description: Any 2xx means you accepted it and ATLAS stops trying

default.description: Anything else is a failure and will be retried

apiKeyAuth.description:
A developer API key, sent as `Authorization: Bearer atl_sk_live_...`. It is a **server-side** secret: ATLAS answers no cross-origin request, so a key a browser can send has already been exposed.

Keys are created in the developer portal and the secret is shown once. Rotating one mints a successor and leaves the old key working for a short overlap; revoking one takes effect on the very next call, because key checks are not cached.

Only the operations that declare this scheme accept a key. Everything else refuses one with 403, identically for the key's own organisation and any other, so the refusal cannot be used to probe what exists.

**Scopes.** Every operation that accepts a key names the one scope it costs, and a key holding a different set is refused `403` with `ATLAS-SYS-007`, naming the scope required. There is no scope meaning "everything", no hierarchy and no implication: `content:write` does not grant `content:read`. An operation that names no scope is one no key reaches.

x-atlas-scopes.content:read: Read your organisation's lectures, courses and their official content
x-atlas-scopes.content:write: Upload new lectures and change your organisation's content
x-atlas-scopes.profiles:read: Read learner profile scores and highlights
x-atlas-scopes.ai:use: Get ATLAS's personalisation recommendations for your learners
x-atlas-scopes.end-users:manage: Link and unlink your own learners
x-atlas-scopes.webhooks:manage: Add, change and remove webhook addresses
x-atlas-scopes.usage:read: Read how much of your allowance your apps have used

delegatedPassAuth.description:
A delegated pass, sent as `Authorization: Bearer eyJ...`. A person signed in, read a consent screen and approved specific permissions; the pass acts **as that person**, limited to what they agreed to.

**The third scheme, and the one whose reach is a person's own data rather than an organisation's.** An API key publishes an organisation and no person. A delegated pass publishes a real ATLAS user, so every row-level rule keyed to that user matches - which is why what a pass may reach is a deliberately short allow-list rather than everything the person can see. Today that is the content-read operations and nothing else, and `x-atlas-scopes` lists exactly the permissions a pass can be granted.

**How to get one.** Send the person to `/oauth/authorize` on the ATLAS web address you were given, with `client_id`, `org_id`, `redirect_uri` (exactly as registered on your application), `scope` (space-separated), `state`, `code_challenge` and `code_challenge_method=S256`. They sign in if they need to, read what you are asking for and decide. On Allow, ATLAS sends them back to your `redirect_uri` with a one-time `code`; your server exchanges it at `exchangeDelegatedToken` (`POST /oauth/token`) together with the `code_verifier`, and renews the pass there with the refresh token. `x-atlas-issued-by` on this scheme names that operation, so a client generator can find the exchange without reading this paragraph. It names an operation for your server to call, never a flow for a tool to run.

**Declared as a bearer token, not as an OAuth flow, and on purpose.** This contract names no host: no environment has a public one yet, and the consent page and the token endpoint are served from different addresses, so no URL written here could be right everywhere. The token exchange also takes JSON rather than RFC 6749's form encoding, so an OAuth flow declared here would send documentation tools and generated clients through an "Authorize" step the endpoint refuses. A tool rendering this contract may accept a pass to send with requests; it must not try to obtain one itself.

**`profiles:read` is not among the permissions**, and will not be by accident: a learner's profile and questionnaire answers are in the tier no plan, setting or role unlocks. Serving them to a third party the person has themselves authorised is a coherent thing to want and a product decision with its own public announcement, not a side effect of building this flow.

**Withdrawal is immediate.** Every request re-reads the grant, so a person who disconnects an application in their settings has disconnected it before its next call - not at the end of the pass's lifetime.

x-atlas-scopes.content:read: Read your organisation's lectures, courses and their official content

RetryAfter.description: Seconds to wait before retrying. Sent with every `429` raised by a request-rate limit. A `429` reporting an exhausted AI credit allowance or a full discussion live-link carries no wait, because neither clears after an interval — see the response-header note in the API description.

RateLimitLimit.description: The caller's own request ceiling for one window. See the response-header note in the API description for when these are sent and what their absence means.

RateLimitRemaining.description: Requests the caller has left in the current window against their overall request rate, floored at zero. Reading it does not consume budget. A `429` raised by a narrower per-operation limit leaves this value unchanged, so it can read a healthy number beside a refusal — see the response-header note in the API description.

RateLimitReset.description: Seconds until the caller's current window ends and the count starts again.

InternalError.description:
An unexpected failure (`ATLAS-SYS-001`). **The one response shape every operation in this API shares**, which is why it is declared on all of them rather than left implicit: a generated client cannot type a failure the contract does not describe.

**Quote the `errorId`.** It is a UUID generated per failure and recorded on the server beside the failure itself, and it is the only thing that connects a report to the cause. Nothing else about the failure crosses the wire — the response never carries internals, stack traces, or any indication of whether the resource involved exists — so `detail` is deliberately the same sentence every time. That is a guarantee rather than a limitation: quote the `errorId` and support can find the rest. A failure the server reports before ATLAS's own handling runs carries the code but no `errorId`, and its `detail` says only that an unexpected error occurred.

Throttled.description:
Too many requests (`ATLAS-SYS-004`): the caller's own request budget for this window is spent, or their organisation's is. Wait `Retry-After` seconds and send the request again; nothing was done.

`RateLimit-Remaining` reads zero on this refusal whichever budget refused - the caller's own, or their organisation's - because zero is what is available to them; `RateLimit-Limit` and `RateLimit-Reset` stay the caller's own. How much an organisation has collectively spent is not something any member's response carries.

This is the request-rate refusal every authenticated operation can answer, declared on each so a generated client can type it. An operation with a narrower budget of its own, or one that spends AI credit, declares that `429` in its own words instead.

RateLimited.description:
Too many requests (problem type `.../problems/rate-limited`, `ATLAS-SYS-004`). Deliberately ONE shape for both the per-IP/global request budget and the account lockout after repeated wrong passwords - the two must be indistinguishable, or the difference would reveal whether an account exists.

On the sign-in endpoints this carries `Retry-After` and **no** rate-limit counters: a remaining count would tell the two cases above apart at a glance and rebuild the difference this shape exists to remove. Authenticated operations that answer with this shape do carry the counters, like every other authenticated response.

ApiScope.description:
One permission an API key can hold. ATLAS publishes the whole vocabulary here, including the names that reach nothing yet: a name that appears later is a new version of the vocabulary, while a name that exists and reaches no operation is a promise this contract can be checked against.

`content:write`, `profiles:read`, `search:use` and `webhooks:manage` are **reserved** at this release and name zero operations. `profiles:read` is reserved for a privacy reason rather than a scheduling one - a learner's profile is in the tier no plan, setting or role unlocks. `webhooks:manage` is reserved for a SECURITY reason: the webhook operations shipped at 1.5.0 and are reachable by a signed-in person only, because changing the address ATLAS dials and reading back what answered are, together, a port scanner - and a key is a credential that may sit in a CI job.

ResourceWebhookEvent.description:
The body of every message ATLAS sends you.

## Verifying it

Every request carries an `ATLAS-Signature` header:

`t=1758499200,v1=5a3f...`

where `t` is a Unix timestamp in seconds and each `v1` is a lower-case hex HMAC-SHA256. To verify:

1. Read the RAW request body as bytes, before any JSON parsing. Parsing
   and re-serialising will change the bytes and the signature will not
   match.

2. Split the header on `,` and read the `t=` value and every `v1=` value.
   There can be MORE THAN ONE `v1` - see rotation below.

3. Build the signed string as `t + "." + body` - the timestamp, a single
   full stop, then the raw body.

4. Compute `HMAC-SHA256(secret, signedString)` with your endpoint's
   signing secret and render it as lower-case hex.

5. Compare it against each `v1` using a CONSTANT-TIME comparison. If any
   matches, the message is authentic.

6. Check that the `t` WHICH PRODUCED THE MATCH is within 300 seconds of
   your own clock. Use that one, not the last `t` you parsed - a header
   can carry more than one, and checking the freshness of a different
   timestamp from the one you verified defeats the window entirely.


## Rotation

When you rotate a signing secret, ATLAS signs with the new secret AND the old one for the overlap window, sending two `v1` values. A verifier that tries every `v1` until one matches - step 5 above - keeps working throughout. A verifier that checks only the first will reject roughly half of what arrives during the window.

## Delivery is at-least-once, and `delivery_id` is how you deduplicate

**You may receive the same message more than once.** That is expected rather than a fault: ATLAS retries a delivery whose outcome it did not observe, and a process that died after your server answered is indistinguishable from one that died before. Exactly-once delivery across a network is not available, and this contract says so rather than implying otherwise.

`delivery_id` is stable for the life of a delivery. Every retry, and every replay you trigger from the webhooks screen, carries the SAME value. Record it and ignore a message whose `delivery_id` you have already processed, and duplicates cost you nothing.

It is inside the signed body, so it cannot be forged or stripped in transit. The `ATLAS-Delivery-Attempt` header carries the attempt number as a convenience for your logs; it is OUTSIDE the signature, so do not make a decision on it.

`event_id` identifies the OCCURRENCE. If you registered two endpoints that feed one system, both will receive the same `event_id` with different `delivery_id`s - deduplicate on `event_id` in that case.

## Ordering

Nothing is promised. A retried `resource.ready` can arrive after the `resource.updated` that superseded it, because a failed delivery waits out its backoff while later ones go straight through. Use `occurred_at`.

## Answering

Any 2xx means accepted. ATLAS waits ten seconds and follows no redirects, so answer as soon as you have durably recorded the message and do the work afterwards. A failure is retried with exponential backoff; after eight attempts the delivery is abandoned and shows in your delivery log, and after five consecutive abandoned deliveries ATLAS stops calling the endpoint until somebody re-enables it.

delivery_id.description: **The value to deduplicate on.** Stable across every retry and replay of this delivery, and inside the bytes the signature covers.

event_id.description: The occurrence. Shared by every endpoint that received this event; use it instead of `delivery_id` if two of your endpoints feed one system.

occurred_at.description: When it happened, UTC. Use this to order, not arrival time.

ResourceWebhookEventData.description: Ids, and one closed vocabulary. No title, no file name, no parser output: this body leaves ATLAS for a machine on the public internet, and nothing derived from an uploaded document travels without a reason. Read the rest with `getResource`, authenticated, under your own scope.

version_id.description: The version this event is about

reason.description: On `resource.failed` only: ATLAS's own name for the stage that refused (for example `EXTRACT_FAILED`). Never a parser message.

TokenExchangeRequest.description: A code exchange, or a renewal. Called by your server; there is no client secret, and PKCE binds the exchange instead.

code.description: The one-time code, for `authorization_code`. Single-use and short-lived.

redirectUri.description: The address the code was sent to. Re-checked against the one recorded with the code (RFC 6749 §4.1.3), which is what stops a code intercepted at one registered address being redeemed as though it had arrived at another.

codeVerifier.description: The verifier your challenge was derived from.

refreshToken.description: The renewal secret, for `refresh_token`. Rotated on every use.

clientId.description: Your application. Re-checked against the code's own record, so a code cannot be redeemed by an application it was not issued to.

DelegatedPassResponse.description: A delegated pass and its renewal secret (RFC 6749 §5.1). The field names are RFC 6749's rather than this document's usual camelCase, because these are the names every OAuth2 client expects to read off a token response.

access_token.description: The pass. Short-lived - but note that what makes a withdrawal take effect is not this lifetime: every delegated request re-reads the grant.

expires_in.description: The pass's remaining life, in seconds.

refresh_token.description: The renewal secret, returned once per issue. Only its SHA-256 is stored. **Presenting a spent one is treated as theft** and revokes every unspent refresh token under the grant.

scope.description: Space-delimited wire names, exactly as the person consented to them.

LinkEndUserRequest.description:
Link one of your own learners. **You are the data controller for this person and ATLAS is your processor**, which is why the only thing this carries is your own reference for them.

ATLAS hashes `ref` and stores the digest. The value itself is never persisted, never logged and never returned - there is no field on any response that could carry it back, and no request that can retrieve it. Send whatever identifier your own system already uses; ATLAS neither needs nor wants to know what it means.

ref.description: Your identifier for this learner. Stable across calls, because the digest of it is what makes two calls the same learner.

EndUserResponse.description: A linked end user. Carries no `ref`, and could not: ATLAS holds only a digest of it.

id.description: What ATLAS will know this learner by on later calls

appId.description: The application that linked them, taken from the key you presented

active.description: False once the link is revoked. A revoked link reaches nothing.

EndUserPage.description: A page of end users (the `{items, nextCursor}` paging envelope). Null `nextCursor` means there is no next page.

PresentEndUserRequest.description:
A personalised read for a linked end user.

**The profile comes with the request, every time.** ATLAS stores no profile for an end user - a learner profile is derived from stored questionnaire answers, and an end user has no ATLAS account to hold any - so this is the input rather than a lookup key. That is also what keeps a retake instant on this surface: there is no cached copy to invalidate, because there is no copy.

DeveloperAppUsage.description: One application's metered activity over the period

name.description: Null when the application has since been removed. Usage outlives what it names, because it is a billing record.

DeveloperRateLimitStanding.description: Where this account stands against its request budget. Reading it does not spend it.

DeveloperUsageState.description: Two named states, decided by ATLAS rather than by the screen, so a client and the filter that actually refuses cannot disagree.

DeveloperUsageResponse.description:
API usage for a developer account. **Carries no figure denominated in money** - commercial data is the account Admin's alone, and it is served by a separate operation this one cannot reach. Operational allowance state is not commercial data, so every role reads this, and so does a key holding `usage:read`.

Two usage panels are absent. **Errors** needs a queryable record of failed requests and ATLAS mints none today; it is tracked and will arrive as an additive change.

calls.description: Metered requests over the period, across every scope

apps.description: The per-app breakdown. Empty when nothing has been metered against an application - an empty list, never a list of zeroes.

KeyIdentityResponse.description:
Who an API key is, and what it may do. It discloses nothing the caller did not already hold - no names, no members, no content, and no permission the presented key does not itself carry - so a stolen key is not also a way to learn about the account it came from.

This is where a `403 ATLAS-SYS-007` is diagnosed: that refusal names the scope it wanted and deliberately never names what your key holds, so the two halves of the answer come from different places and only the holder can put them together.

orgId.description: The developer account this key belongs to

scopes.description: What this key may do. Fixed when the key was minted - widening is a new key and narrowing is a revoke - so this is the set every call you make will be judged against.

ResourceListResponse.description: One page of the org's resource library, with the totals pagination controls need.

totalItems.description: How many resources match in the whole org

totalPages.description: How many pages that is at this size; at least 1, so an empty library reads as one empty page rather than none

ResourceDownloadResponse.description: A short-lived URL for a resource's original file. Returned as a URL in a JSON body rather than a redirect, so the browser never follows a cross-origin redirect with credentials attached and the screen can surface a failure as a message.

downloadUrl.description: The presigned GET URL; forces attachment + application/octet-stream so untrusted uploaded bytes can never render as markup

expiresAt.description: When it lapses; re-request rather than caching it

filename.description: The name the browser will save it under

ResourceResponse.description:
A resource's state - its identity plus the state of its DISPLAY version (the current one when set, else its latest) flattened in, so the library and detail surfaces read one object per resource. `status`, `sizeBytes`, `contentType`, and `originalFilename` describe the display version; `versionCount` is the whole timeline's length.

The bytes' `fingerprint` is deliberately NOT here. It would be harmless as a per-org detail - a member who can list a resource can download it and hash it themselves - but it is the platform-wide key that content-addressed reuse is decided on, and a stable cross-org content identifier on a bulk listing lets two members in DIFFERENT orgs establish that both orgs hold the same file, byte for byte. That is what ATLAS refuses to let anyone learn by timing, reached another way.

status.description: Where the display version stands in the upload state machine: uploading (AWAITING_UPLOAD) -> virus-scan (SCANNING) -> reading/extracting (READING) -> building (BUILDING) -> ready (READY), or FAILED with a `failureReason`. READING and BUILDING are ingestion states: the finalize call returns READING and the rest happens asynchronously, so a client that needs the settled outcome polls. A version becomes the resource's current one only on READY, which is why a resource can show a READY display version while a NEWER one of its versions is still READING.

failureReason.description: Why the resource failed; null unless `status` is FAILED. TOO_LARGE = over the upload size ceiling. INFECTED = a malware signature matched. ARCHIVE_LIMITS = the content defeated the scanner's archive limits and could not be fully inspected (a zip bomb, for example) - unscannable is rejected, not trusted. SCAN_REQUIRED = uploaded before virus scanning existed, so it was never scanned; re-upload it. UPLOAD_ABANDONED = the upload was never finished and has been swept; its object, if any, was discarded. UPLOAD_MISMATCHED = the stored object was not the one the upload was authorised for (its size differed from the length signed into the URL), so it was discarded - distinct from TOO_LARGE because it may be smaller. EXTRACT_FAILED = the bytes scanned clean but the document reader could not turn them into a block tree: encrypted, corrupt, no text layer, or past the structural bounds. Its object is KEPT, unlike every reason above it, so a better extractor can make the same file work later without asking the uploader to find it again - but the outcome of THIS version is terminal, like all the others. BLOCKED = the file's fingerprint is on the takedown blocklist, so ATLAS declines to host these bytes for anyone; its object is discarded, and the remedy is an appeal rather than a re-upload, which would be refused identically. INGEST_ABANDONED = the document reader was handed this version repeatedly and never reported back - the one reason that blames ATLAS rather than the file or its standing, so its object is KEPT and the advice is simply to upload again. Distinct from EXTRACT_FAILED, where a reader DID look at the bytes. Names the category only, never the matched signature and never the parser's own message.

sizeBytes.description: The stored size in bytes; null before receipt

contentType.description: The stored content type; null before receipt

versionNumber.description: The display version's position in the timeline (1..N)

versionCount.description: How many versions the resource has (1 means no history yet)

updatedAt.description: When the display version last changed state

deletedAt.description: When the resource was moved to the trash, or null for a live one. Only the trash listing and the restore response ever carry this non-null - every other surface refuses a trashed resource as absent - so a client reading it can show how much of the grace period is left.

LearnerProfile.description: A learner's scored profile. Personal data in the most private tier - never visible to an org in any form. Returned from the stored answers on every read, with no stored copy to go stale; sent by a developer to `presentForEndUser`, where it is held to the instrument and to the bounds below.

completedDimensions.description: The areas these numbers cover, in canonical order - computed from the answers, never accepted from a request. An area absent here was not scored at all, rather than scored low.

categoryScores.description: `subDimension.category` to its 1-5 mean, rounded to 4 dp, e.g. `D1.Read/Write`. Insertion order is the taxonomy's order.

percentScores.description: The same keys on a 0-100 scale, 2 dp, computed from the ROUNDED mean - the order of those two roundings is part of the scoring contract.

subDimensionScores.description: Sub-dimension code to its score. `structureType` discriminates the two shapes: a multi-category sub-dimension yields one score per category and a dominant category; a bipolar one yields a single combined score where 5 is strongly pole A, 1 is strongly pole B and 3 is balanced.

categories.description: Each category's own 1-5 mean, so the categories can be ranked

dominantCategory.description: The first strict maximum in canonical category order, so a tie resolves to the taxonomy rather than to whatever a sort happened to do

score.description: 5 is strongly pole A, 1 is strongly pole B and 3 is balanced.

AttentionChecksSummary.description: The validity signal from the sitting's attention checks. It is not a score and changes nothing - a respondent who fails every check still gets exactly the profile their answers produce.

presented.description: Checks DRAWN into a round, answered or not - so this may exceed `passed + failed`. That gap is the whole point: a check shown and skipped is the signal a tally derived from answers alone cannot see.

PersonalisationProfile.description: What ATLAS personalises for one learner, and why. Private to the learner, derived on every read and stored nowhere.

signature.description:
The short code summarising the profile, used to reuse AI work between similar learners - `v1:<taxonomyVersion>:<34 band characters>`, one per subscale in canonical order, `-` where unscored.

SERVER-DERIVED ONLY. No ATLAS endpoint accepts this value, and none ever will: it keys the platform-wide transformation cache, so a route that took it from a client would let a caller read or poison another cohort's cached rewrites, across orgs. Treat it as opaque and do not send it back.

ABSENT (omitted, never sent as null) when the learner has completed nothing - and absence is not the same as a code of all dashes: it means "do not reuse anything on the strength of this", where a dashes-only code would pool every unprofiled learner onto one cache entry.

SO ITS PRESENCE IS THE SECOND HALF OF THE GATE ON EVERY `AI` FAMILY, alongside that feature's `enabled`. Absence here and a `204` from the re-presentation routes are the same fact, derived by the same server-side call - a client that reads `enabled` alone offers a control the api can only ever refuse.

completedDimensions.description: The areas these recommendations rest on, canonical order

endorsements.description: The preferences the answers actually expressed, in the instrument's canonical order. Only ONE pole of a bipolar sub-dimension can ever appear - a single score cannot endorse both ends of its own line - and a category at or below the scale's midpoint appears not at all.

features.description: All 21 families in recommendation order, recommended or not

PresentationPlan.description:
What the reader should do differently for this learner, with no AI and no wait. Always present and never null: every option carries an explicit baseline value, so "the profile has no view" is a state the plan states rather than one a client infers from absence.

**Only `figures` is rendered today.** The rest carry the learner's preference and are applied by nobody yet - `chunking` and `navigation` need a reader surface that does not exist yet, and `tableOfContents` and `panels` are simply unconsumed. No feature family gates them - F2, F3, F6 and F10 are all live; nothing reads them.

`panels` stays unrendered by decision rather than by omission: Zone 7 is its own route, and the reader's utility rail is exactly three tabs with no social panel in it, so wiring a fourth from this value would build a surface the reader does not have. A value here is what the learner prefers, not permission to show it: whoever renders one applies its gate at that point.

**Disagreement resolves to the baseline.** Presentation options are not additive - a chunk is either small or whole - so where two endorsed categories disagree the presenter applies neither. The reasoning is a research one: a precedence rule invented in code would rank learner profiles against one another in a way the research never does.

figures.description: Whether figures lead the prose they illustrate. The one option the reader applies today, gated on F12.

chunking.description: How much is presented at once. `whole-document` and `source-default` render alike today and are deliberately distinct: one is "this learner wants the whole thing", the other is "ATLAS has no view".

navigation.description: Whether a path is recommended or the learner roams.

tableOfContents.description: Whether the contents list is foregrounded. `suppressed` means collapsed with the affordance intact - the report's principle 3 is that nothing is withheld.

panels.description: Whether the side panels are foregrounded, on the same terms.

EndorsedCategory.description: One preference the learner expressed, and what it recommends - grouped per category.

label.description: The reader-facing row name, e.g. "Sound: Quiet" - already disambiguated within its area, which is why a panel shows this rather than the bare category code.

strength.description:
How strongly this is endorsed, on the instrument's own 1-5 scale, so a screen can say "strongly" or "slightly" without a second rule.

For a POLE this is the sub-dimension's score REFLECTED onto that pole (`6 - score` for the low end), so 5 always means "strongly this" at either end of a line. Do not compare it back to the raw bipolar score.

weight.description: `(strength - 3) / 2`, in (0, 1] - what this contributes to each family

families.description: The families this category marks, in the LEARNER'S recommendation order rather than catalogue order.

RecommendedFeature.description: One feature family placed in this learner's recommendation order.

rank.description: 1-based place. TIED SCORES SHARE A RANK and the next place skips (1, 2, 2, 4) - printing "2nd" and "3rd" for two equal scores would claim a difference the engine does not have.

kind.description:
WHICH OF THE TWO FEATURE CATALOGUES this family comes from - provenance, and nothing more.

This field used to be described here as "an `AI` family costs the org's allowance, is RAG-grounded and AI-chip-labelled, and degrades to plain content on a provider outage". Those are claims about MECHANISM, and `A6` disproves all four: it is in the AI catalogue and computes light maths over the learner's own attempt records with no gateway call at all. A client that gated an AI affordance on this value told the learner so - see `usesModel`, which is the field for that question.

usesModel.description:
WHETHER THIS FAMILY'S OUTPUT ACTUALLY COMES FROM A MODEL - what the cyan ✦ AI chip asserts, and the field a client must gate that chip on rather than on `kind`.

True for every AI-catalogue family except `A6`. Read this for anything that is really about a model running: an over-quota explanation, a "this was AI-generated" label, a degradation notice. Read `kind` only for grouping by the report's catalogue.

delivery.description:
Whether anything consumes this family YET - not whether the feature exists. Search and free navigation exist; neither is profile-driven, so recommending them changes nothing a learner sees.

`LIVE` at the time of writing: `F1`, `F2`, `F3`, `F4`, `F5`, `F6`, `F7`, `F10`, `F11`, `F12`, `F13`, `A1`, `A2`, `A3`, `A4`, `A5`, `A6`, `A8`. This list goes stale on every promotion and the response is the arbiter: read this field rather than the list.

score.description: The score-weighted union: the sum of the weights of the endorsed categories marking it. Zero when nothing endorsed it.

autoEnabled.description:
Whether the ENGINE switched it on at setup. Requires an endorsing category at 4.0 or better ("Agree"), AND that the family is not opt-in-only, AND that it is `LIVE`. Never true for `F8` or `A8`.

UNAFFECTED BY THE LEARNER'S OWN CHOICE - it stays the engine's answer, so a panel can still say "recommended for you" about something the learner switched off. Read `enabled` for the state to render a toggle in.

override.description:
The learner's own choice - the learner has full control, OMITTED when they have never made one.

Absent and `false` are different states and a client must not collapse them: absent means the engine's answer stands, `false` means the learner said no. That distinction is what makes "reset to recommended" expressible - clearing an override is `null` on the PATCH, and it comes back as this field being absent again.

enabled.description:
WHAT THE LEARNER ACTUALLY RECEIVES, and the field a single on/off control should be bound to: the `override` when there is one, otherwise `autoEnabled`.

Never true for a `PLANNED` family whatever is stored - "enabled" must not describe something no part of the product reads. Note the asymmetry with `autoEnabled` for the opt-in-only families: `F8` and `A8` are never auto-enabled at any score (rule 5), but an explicit `override` of `true` IS honoured, because that is the opt-in the rule is named for.

IT IS NOT SUFFICIENT ON ITS OWN FOR A FAMILY WHOSE `kind` IS `AI`. Those features personalise FROM the profile, so they additionally require `signature` to be present: with no signature there is nothing to key the transformation cache on, and the re-presentation routes answer `204` whatever this field says. The two are not redundant - an override is stored in its own table and survives a retake that erases the answers, so `enabled: true` with no `signature` is an ordinary state and not a malformed one. Bind an AI control to BOTH, or it offers something that can never work.

reasons.description: The endorsing categories, strongest first; empty when not recommended

FeatureReason.description: Why a family was recommended - the preference that asked for it

ProfileAppearanceDefaults.description: Look-and-feel settings the profile SUGGESTS - defaults, never saved choices. `/appearance/preferences` stays the record of what the person actually chose; resolve explicit choice, then these, then the client's own default. A field the profile says nothing about is OMITTED, never sent as null - the same convention `/appearance/preferences` uses, so a client resolving the layers reads one shape rather than two. Most settings are always absent: no sub-dimension measures text size, line spacing or reading face.

theme.description: From OD2's Light sub-dimension - strongly Bright suggests light, strongly Dim dark

focusMode.description: True when OD2's Sound reading is strongly Quiet. NEVER false: the spec states one direction, and a preference for noise says nothing about focus mode the engine may state.

Problem.description:
Problem details (RFC 9457, `application/problem+json`), the one shape every refusal in this API takes.

**Branch on `errorCode`.** It is present on every refusal (the API description names the one malformed path the web server refuses first), it names one cause exactly, every value is documented in this contract - on the operations that can answer it, or in the API description for the few that any operation can - and a value is never removed or reused once published. A new value is a minor version of this contract. `type` is coarser: two causes can share one - `not-found` covers both a missing record and an organisation that is not a developer account - so a client branching on `type` would treat them alike.

**`type` is an identifier, not a link.** It is a URI under `https://atlasframework.dev/problems/`, stable for as long as its code is, and fine to compare and to log. Do not dereference it: no page is published at those addresses yet.

Validation refusals add an `errors` array naming each field; an unexpected `500` adds an `errorId`, which is what to quote when reporting it.

type.description: An identifier for the kind of problem - compare it, never fetch it. See the schema description.

errorCode.description: What to branch on: `ATLAS-<MODULE>-<NNN>`, one cause each, e.g. `ATLAS-AUTH-005`. Present on every refusal.

errorId.description: Present on unexpected 500s; correlates to the server log
